lede: A grouped table says how many eggs weigh between 50 g and 55 g. It never says how many weigh under 55 g, which is usually what you want to know. Add the classes as you go down and each total answers that question; plot the totals and the curve answers it for every mass on the axis.
can: Turn a frequency column into a column of running totals.
Plot each running total at the upper boundary of its class.
Read a median, the quartiles and a count off the curve.

text: Cumulative frequency: how many so far

md: A **cumulative frequency** is a running total. Add the classes as you go down the table and each entry answers one question: how many values are **this much or less**. Plot those totals against the top of each class, join them with one smooth curve, and the graph answers that question for every value on the axis, not only at the class boundaries.

prompt: The frequencies of the first three classes are 5, 20 and 20. What is the third cumulative frequency?
explain: $5 + 20 + 20 = 45$. Each entry is the total so far, not the class on its own.

md:
Here is the egg table with the running totals filled in. The question that decides the whole graph is: which mass does each total belong above?

Take the total 45 for the class $50 < m \le 55$. It counts every egg of mass 55 g or less. At 50 g that class has not been counted at all; at 52.5 g only part of it has. The total is only true at the **top** of the class, so 45 is plotted at $m = 55$.

That single decision is where the plotting mark lives, and in Summer 2025 upper bounds, midpoints and lower bounds turned up in roughly equal numbers.

prompt: The running total after the fifth class is 76 and the last class has frequency 4. What is the final cumulative frequency?
explain: $76 + 4 = 80$, and that must equal the number of eggs, which is the check that the whole column is right.

prompt: At which value of $m$ is the running total for the class $60 < m \le 65$ plotted?
explain: The upper class boundary. At 60 g the class has not started; the total is only complete at 65 g.

title: Not on the formula sheet
md:
Plot each running total at the **upper class boundary**.

Median: read across from $\tfrac{n}{2}$. Lower quartile: $\tfrac{n}{4}$. Upper quartile: $\tfrac{3n}{4}$. $\text{IQR} = \text{UQ} - \text{LQ}$.

The page-2 Higher formula sheet carries no statistics formulae, so all of this is recall.

prompt: Fill the gap: each cumulative frequency is plotted at the ______ class boundary.
explain: Upper. The running total is only complete at the top of the class.

text: Reading the median and the quartiles

md:
The curve is read **across first, then down**. Start on the cumulative frequency axis, because that axis counts values.

With $n = 80$ eggs: the median is the $40$th, so go across from $40$. The lower quartile is the $20$th, the upper quartile the $60$th.

The common wreck is to halve the horizontal axis instead. For these eggs that would give 55 g, and the real median is about $53.75$ g. Halving the axis halves the masses; the median halves the eggs.

prompt: What joins the points on a cumulative frequency diagram?
options: One smooth curve through the points in order
Bars from the axis up to each point
A line of best fit that need not touch the points
answer: One smooth curve through the points in order
explain: A curve, and it passes through every plotted point. In November 2024 a bar chart scored nothing and also removed the follow-through marks from the part that read the graph.

prompt: A cumulative frequency curve is drawn for 60 people. At what height do you read across for the upper quartile?
explain: $\tfrac{3 \times 60}{4} = 45$. Three quarters of the people lie below the upper quartile.

prompt: From the picture above, what is the interquartile range of the egg masses, in grams?

title: Why a reading off a grid line is still a good answer
md: The curve is an estimate built from grouped data, so the answer is an estimate too. Summer 2024 M4 Q10 says it outright: when a reading falls between two grid lines, a value in between is exactly what is wanted. Refusing to commit is what loses the mark, not the odd tenth.

title: Drawing Cumulative Frequency Graphs
why: The table-to-graph routine at a steady pace. Watch where each point is placed: the running total goes above the top of its class every time.

prompt: In the video, each cumulative frequency is plotted against which value?
answer: The upper boundary of its class
explain: Yes. That is the one decision the plotting mark tests.
options: The upper boundary of its class

md:
The curve always counts **downwards**: the height above a value is the number of items that are that value or less.

- **Below** a value: read straight off the curve.
- **Above** a value: read the curve, then subtract from the total.
- **Between** two values: read the curve twice and subtract the smaller reading from the larger.

For the eggs, the reading at 60 g is 65, so the number heavier than 60 g is $80 - 65 = 15$. November 2024 M3 Q27 reports that only the strongest candidates read both values and subtracted.

prompt: A curve for 50 journeys reads 12 at 24 minutes and 43 at 38 minutes. How many journeys took between 24 and 38 minutes?
explain: $43 - 12 = 31$. Between two values is the difference of the two readings, never one of them on its own.

md:
An axis marked **Price (£1000s)** or **Value, $V$ (£1000s)** counts thousands. A reading of 9 on such an axis is £9000, not £9.

Both Summer 2025 reports name this: candidates found the quartiles correctly, subtracted correctly, and then wrote an answer a thousand times too small. Read the axis label out loud before the answer line is filled in.

prompt: On an axis marked Price (£1000s) the quartiles read 155 and 245. What is the interquartile range, in pounds?
explain: $245 - 155 = 90$ on the axis, and each unit is £1000, so the interquartile range is £90 000.

prompt: A class is $20 < t \le 25$ and its running total is 33. At which value of $t$ is the point plotted?
explain: The upper class boundary. The running total of 33 is only complete once every value up to 25 has been counted.

title: Bars cost the next part as well
md: November 2024 M4 Q13(b) reports that a bar chart scored nothing in that part and left nothing to carry into part (c). One wrong diagram removed the marks from a part that only needed a reading.

prompt: A candidate draws a bar chart in part (b). What happens in part (c), which reads from the graph?
options: Nothing in part (b), and nothing to carry into part (c)
Part (b) scores nothing but part (c) still follows through
answer: Nothing in part (b), and nothing to carry into part (c)
explain: One wrong diagram takes the marks from a part that only needed a reading. That is the November 2024 M4 finding in one line.

md:
Fill in a cumulative frequency column of running totals.
Plot each total at the upper boundary of its class.
Read the median and the quartiles across from the frequency axis.
Count above, below or between by subtracting two readings.

Three parts run together: complete the running totals, draw the curve on the printed grid, then read something off it. The first mark is the totals, the last of which must equal the number of items; the reading marks follow through from your own curve. Stuck: draw the dashed lines across from the frequency axis anyway — a visible reading line shows the method, and the marker credits what is on the page.
